transcript.text: Good morning. You’re through to the tourist information office, Tim speaking. How can I help you?
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: Oh hello. Could you give me some information about next month’s festival, please? My family and I will be staying in the town that week.
transcript.speaker: JEAN

transcript.text: Of course. Well it starts with a concert on the afternoon of the 17th.
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: Oh I heard about that. The orchestra and singers come from the USA, don’t they?
transcript.speaker: JEAN

transcript.text: They’re from Canada. They’re very popular over there. They’re going to perform a number of well-known pieces that will appeal to children as well as adults.
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: That sounds good. My whole family are interested in music.
transcript.speaker: JEAN

transcript.text: The next day, the 18th, there’s a performance by a ballet company called Eustatis.
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: Sorry?
transcript.speaker: JEAN

transcript.text: The name is spelt E-U-S-T-A-T-I-S. They appeared in last year’s festival, and went down very well. Again, their programme is designed for all ages.
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: Good. I expect we’ll go to that. I hope there’s going to be a play during the festival, a comedy, ideally.
transcript.speaker: JEAN

transcript.text: You’re in luck! On the 19th and 20th a local amateur group are performing one written by a member of group. It’s called Jemima. That’ll be on in the town hall. They’ve already performed it two or three times. I haven’t seen it myself, but the review in the local paper was very good.
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: And is it suitable for children?
transcript.speaker: JEAN

transcript.text: Yes, in fact it’s aimed more at children than at adults, so both performances are in the afternoon.
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: And what about dance? Will there be any performances?
transcript.speaker: JEAN

transcript.text: Yes, also on the 20th, but in the evening. A professional company is putting on a show of modern pieces, with electronic music by young composers.
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: Uh-huh.
transcript.speaker: JEAN

transcript.text: The show is about how people communicate, or fail to communicate, with each other, so it’s got the rather strange name, Chat.
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: I suppose that’s because that’s something we do both face to face and online.
transcript.speaker: JEAN

transcript.text: That’s right.
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: Now there are also some workshops and other activities. They’ll all take place at least once every day, so everyone who wants to take part will have a chance.
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: Good. We’re particularly interested in cookery – you don’t happen to have a cookery workshop, do you?
transcript.speaker: JEAN

transcript.text: We certainly do. It’s going to focus on how to make food part of a healthy lifestyle, and it’ll show that even sweet things like cakes can contain much less sugar than they usually do.
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: That might be worth going to. We’re trying to encourage our children to cook.
transcript.speaker: JEAN

transcript.text: Another workshop is just for children, and that’s on creating posters to reflect the history of the town. The aim is to make children aware of how both the town and people’s lives have changed over the centuries. The results will be exhibited in the community centre. Then the other workshop is in toy-making, and that’s for adults only.
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: Oh, why’s that?
transcript.speaker: JEAN

transcript.text: Because it involves carpentry – participants will be making toys out of wood, so there’ll be a lot of sharp chisels and other tools around.
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: It makes sense to keep children away from it.
transcript.speaker: JEAN

transcript.text: Exactly. Now let me tell you about some of the outdoor activities. There’ll be supervised wild swimming …
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: Wild swimming? What’s that?
transcript.speaker: JEAN

transcript.text: It just means swimming in natural waters, rather than a swimming pool.
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: Oh OK. In a lake, for instance.
transcript.speaker: JEAN

transcript.text: Yes, there’s a beautiful one just outside the town, and that’ll be the venue for the swimming. There’ll be lifeguards on duty, so it’s suitable for all ages. And finally, there’ll be a walk in some nearby woods every day. The leader is an expert on insects. He’ll show some that live in the woods, and how important they are for the environment. So there are going to be all sorts of different things to do during the festival.
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: There certainly are.
transcript.speaker: JEAN

transcript.text: If you’d like to read about how the preparations for the festival are going, the festival organizer is keeping a blog. Just search online for the festival website, and you’ll find it.
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: Well, thank you very much for all the information.
transcript.speaker: JEAN

transcript.text: You’re welcome. Goodbye.
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: Goodbye.
transcript.speaker: JEAN

transcript.text: I’m very pleased to welcome this evening’s guest speaker, Mark Logan, who’s going to tell us about the recent transformation of Minster Park.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Over to you, Mark.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Thank you.
transcript.speaker: MARK

transcript.text: I’m sure you’re all familiar with Minster Park.
transcript.speaker: MARK

transcript.text: It’s been a feature of the city for well over a century, and has been the responsibility of the city council for most of that time.
transcript.speaker: MARK

transcript.text: What perhaps isn’t so well known is the origin of the park: unlike many public parks that started in private ownership, as the garden of a large house, for instance, Minster was some waste land, which people living nearby started planting with flowers in 1892.
transcript.speaker: MARK

transcript.text: It was unclear who actually owned the land, and this wasn’t settled until 20 years later, when the council took possession of it.
transcript.speaker: MARK

transcript.text: You may have noticed the statue near one of the entrances.
transcript.speaker: MARK

transcript.text: It’s of Diane Gosforth, who played a key role in the history of the park.
transcript.speaker: MARK

transcript.text: Once the council had become the legal owner, it planned to sell the land for housing.
transcript.speaker: MARK

transcript.text: Many local people wanted it to remain a place that everyone could go to, to enjoy the fresh air and natural environment – remember the park is in a densely populated residential area.
transcript.speaker: MARK

transcript.text: Diane Gosforth was one of those people, and she organised petitions and demonstrations, which eventually made the council change its mind about the future of the land.
transcript.speaker: MARK

transcript.text: Soon after this the First World War broke out, in 1914, and most of the park was dug up and planted with vegetables, which were sold locally.
transcript.speaker: MARK

transcript.text: At one stage the army considered taking it over for troop exercises and got as far as contacting the city council, then decided the park was too small to be of use.
transcript.speaker: MARK

transcript.text: There were occasional public meetings during the war, in an area that had been retained as grass.
transcript.speaker: MARK

transcript.text: After the war, the park was turned back more or less to how it had been before 1914, and continued almost unchanged until recently.
transcript.speaker: MARK

transcript.text: Plans for transforming it were drawn up at various times, most recently in 2013, though they were revised in 2015, before any work had started.
transcript.speaker: MARK

transcript.text: The changes finally got going in 2016, and were finished on schedule last year.
transcript.speaker: MARK

transcript.text: OK, let me tell you about some of the changes that have been made – and some things that have been retained.
transcript.speaker: MARK

transcript.text: If you look at this map, you’ll see the familiar outline of the park, with the river forming the northern boundary, and a gate in each of the other three walls.
transcript.speaker: MARK

transcript.text: The statue of Diane Gosforth has been moved: it used to be close to the south gate, but it’s now immediately to the north of the lily pond, almost in the centre of the park, which makes it much more visible.
transcript.speaker: MARK

transcript.text: There’s a new area of wooden sculptures, which are on the river bank, where the path from the east gate makes a sharp bend.
transcript.speaker: MARK

transcript.text: There are two areas that are particularly intended for children.
transcript.speaker: MARK

transcript.text: The playground has been enlarged and improved, and that’s between the river and the path that leads from the pond to the river.
transcript.speaker: MARK

transcript.text: Then there’s a new maze, a circular series of paths, separated by low hedges.
transcript.speaker: MARK

transcript.text: That’s near the west gate – you go north from there towards the river and then turn left to reach it.
transcript.speaker: MARK

transcript.text: There have been tennis courts in the park for many years, and they’ve been doubled, from four to eight.
transcript.speaker: MARK

transcript.text: They’re still in the south-west corner of the park, where there’s a right-angle bend in the path.
transcript.speaker: MARK

transcript.text: Something else I’d like to mention is the new fitness area.
transcript.speaker: MARK

transcript.text: This is right next to the lily pond on the same side as the west gate.
transcript.speaker: MARK

transcript.text: Now, as you’re all gardeners, I’m sure you’ll like to hear about the plants that have been chosen for the park.
transcript.speaker: MARK

transcript.text: OK, Graham, so let’s check we both know what we’re supposed to be doing.
transcript.speaker: CATHY

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: GRAHAM

transcript.text: So, for the university’s open day, we have to plan a display on British life and literature in the mid-19th century.
transcript.speaker: CATHY

transcript.text: That’s right. But we’ll have some people to help us find the materials and set it up, remember – for the moment, we just need to plan it.
transcript.speaker: GRAHAM

transcript.text: Good. So have you gathered who’s expected to come and see the display? Is it for the people studying English, or students from other departments? I’m not clear about it.
transcript.speaker: CATHY

transcript.text: Nor me. That was how it used to be, but it didn’t attract many people, so this year it’s going to be part of an open day, to raise the university’s profile. It’ll be publicised in the city, to encourage people to come and find out something of what goes on here. And it’s included in the information that’s sent to people who are considering applying to study here next year.
transcript.speaker: GRAHAM

transcript.text: Presumably some current students and lecturers will come?
transcript.speaker: CATHY

transcript.text: I would imagine so, but we’ve been told to concentrate on the other categories of people.
transcript.speaker: GRAHAM

transcript.text: Right. We don’t have to cover the whole range of 19th-century literature, do we?
transcript.speaker: CATHY

transcript.text: No, it’s entirely up to us. I suggest just using Charles Dickens.
transcript.speaker: GRAHAM

transcript.text: That’s a good idea. Most people have heard of him, and have probably read some of his novels, or seen films based on them, so that’s a good lead-in to life in his time.
transcript.speaker: CATHY

transcript.text: Exactly. And his novels show the awful conditions that most people had to live in, don’t they: he wanted to shock people into doing something about it.
transcript.speaker: GRAHAM

transcript.text: Did he do any campaigning, other than writing?
transcript.speaker: CATHY

transcript.text: Yes, he campaigned for education and other social reforms, and gave talks, but I’m inclined to ignore that and focus on the novels.
transcript.speaker: GRAHAM

transcript.text: Yes, I agree.
transcript.speaker: CATHY

transcript.text: OK, so now shall we think about a topic linked to each novel?
transcript.speaker: CATHY

transcript.text: Yes. I’ve printed out a list of Dickens’s novels in the order they were published, in the hope you’d agree to focus on him!
transcript.speaker: GRAHAM

transcript.text: You’re lucky I did agree! Let’s have a look. OK, the first was The Pickwick Papers, published in 1836. It was very successful when it came out, wasn’t it, and was adapted for the theatre straight away.
transcript.speaker: CATHY

transcript.text: There’s an interesting point, though, that there’s a character who keeps falling asleep, and that medical condition was named after the book – Pickwickian Syndrome.
transcript.speaker: GRAHAM

transcript.text: Oh, so why don’t we use that as the topic, and include some quotations from the novel?
transcript.speaker: CATHY

transcript.text: Right, Next is Oliver Twist. There’s a lot in the novel about poverty. But maybe something less obvious …
transcript.speaker: GRAHAM

transcript.text: Well Oliver is taught how to steal, isn’t he? We could use that to illustrate the fact that very few children went to school, particularly not poor children, so they learnt in other ways.
transcript.speaker: CATHY

transcript.text: Good idea. What’s next?
transcript.speaker: GRAHAM

transcript.text: Maybe Nicholas Nickleby. Actually he taught in a really cruel school, didn’t he?
transcript.speaker: CATHY

transcript.text: That’s right. But there’s also the company of touring actors that Nicholas joins. We could do something on theatres and other amusements of the time. We don’t want only the bad things, do we?
transcript.speaker: GRAHAM

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: CATHY

transcript.text: What about Martin Chuzzlewit? He goes to the USA, doesn’t he?
transcript.speaker: GRAHAM

transcript.text: Yes, and Dickens himself had been there a year before, and drew on his experience there in the novel.
transcript.speaker: CATHY

transcript.text: I wonder, though … The main theme is selfishness, so we could do something on social justice? No, too general, let’s keep to your idea – I think it would work well.
transcript.speaker: GRAHAM

transcript.text: He wrote Bleak House next – that’s my favourite of his novels.
transcript.speaker: CATHY

transcript.text: Yes, mine too. His satire of the legal system is pretty powerful.
transcript.speaker: GRAHAM

transcript.text: That’s true, but think about Esther, the heroine. As a child she lives with someone she doesn’t know is her aunt, who treats her very badly. Then she’s very happy living with her guardian, and he puts her in charge of the household. And at the end she gets married and her guardian gives her and her husband a house, where of course they’re very happy.
transcript.speaker: CATHY

transcript.text: Yes, I like that.
transcript.speaker: GRAHAM

transcript.text: What shall we take next? Little Dorrit? Old Mr Dorrit has been in a debtors’ prison for years …
transcript.speaker: CATHY

transcript.text: So was Dickens’s father, wasn’t he?
transcript.speaker: GRAHAM

transcript.text: That’s right.
transcript.speaker: CATHY

transcript.text: What about focusing on the part when Mr Dorrit inherits a fortune, and he starts pretending he’s always been rich?
transcript.speaker: GRAHAM

transcript.text: Good idea.
transcript.speaker: CATHY

transcript.text: OK, so next we need to think about what materials we want to illustrate each issue. That’s going to be quite hard.
transcript.speaker: GRAHAM

transcript.text: I’m going to report on a case study of a programme which has been set up to help rural populations in Mozambique, a largely agricultural country in South-East Africa.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The programme worked with three communities in Chicualacuala district, near the Limpopo River.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This is a dry and arid region, with unpredictable rainfall.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Because of this, people in the area were unable to support themselves through agriculture and instead they used the forest as a means of providing themselves with an income, mainly by selling charcoal.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: However, this was not a sustainable way of living in the long term, as they were rapidly using up this resource.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: To support agriculture in this dry region, the programme focused primarily on making use of existing water resources from the Limpopo River by setting up systems of irrigation, which would provide a dependable water supply for crops and animals.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The programme worked closely with the district government in order to find the best way of implementing this.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The region already had one farmers’ association, and it was decided to set up two more of these.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: These associations planned and carried out activities including water management, livestock breeding and agriculture, and it was notable that in general, women formed the majority of the workforce.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: It was decided that in order to keep the crops safe from animals, both wild and domestic, special areas should be fenced off where the crops could be grown.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The community was responsible for creating these fences, but the programme provided the necessary wire for making them.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Once the area had been fenced off, it could be cultivated.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The land was dug, so that vegetables and cereals appropriate to the climate could be grown, and the programme provided the necessary seeds for this.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The programme also provided pumps so that water could be brought from the river in pipes to the fields.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: However, the labour was all provided by local people, and they also provided and put up the posts that supported the fences around the fields.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Once the programme had been set up, its development was monitored carefully.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The farmers were able to grow enough produce not just for their own needs, but also to sell.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: However, getting the produce to places where it could be marketed was sometimes a problem, as the farmers did not have access to transport, and this resulted in large amounts of produce, especially vegetables, being spoiled.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This problem was discussed with the farmers’ associations and it was decided that in order to prevent food from being spoiled, the farmers needed to learn techniques for its preservation.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: There was also an additional initiative that had not been originally planned, but which became a central feature of the programme.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This was when farmers started to dig holes for tanks in the fenced-off areas and to fill these with water and use them for breeding fish – an important source of protein.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: After a time, another suggestion was made by local people which hadn’t been part of the programme’s original proposal, but which was also adopted later on.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: They decided to try setting up colonies of bees, which would provide honey both for their own consumption and to sell.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: So what lessons can be learned from this programme?
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: First of all, it tells us that in dry, arid regions, if there is access to a reliable source of water, there is great potential for the development of agriculture.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: In Chicualacuala, there was a marked improvement in agricultural production, which improved food security and benefited local people by providing them with both food and income.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: However, it’s important to set realistic timelines for each phase of the programme, especially for its design, as mistakes made at this stage may be hard to correct later on.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The programme demonstrates that sustainable development is possible in areas where …
transcript.speaker: LECTURER
